content: Overmedication occurs when a healthcare provider prescribes medications that are unnecessary or in excessive amounts for a patient. This situation may arise due to a lack of awareness on the part of the doctor regarding other medications the patient is already taking. It can also result from insufficient knowledge about how a particular drug interacts with other substances or specific populations, or simply due to human error. In some cases, overmedication is intentional and may even be illegal, such as when excessive psychoactive drugs are used as chemical restraints for elderly individuals in nursing homes. The potential side effects of overmedication include slowed reaction times, which can affect speech, movement, and thought processes. Patients may also experience sleeplessness, increased confusion, and an unsteady gait. Other possible adverse effects include constipation, dry mouth, blurry vision, heightened agitation, and involuntary repetitive movements of the tongue, feet, hands, or trunk. In severe cases, hallucinations may occur. Overmedication is not limited to errors by healthcare providers. It can also happen when patients or caregivers administer more medication than prescribed or recommended on over-the-counter (OTC) product labels. This may occur either intentionally or unintentionally. For example, a patient taking a prescription medication like Vicodin, which contains both hydrocodone and acetaminophen, might unknowingly take an OTC product like Tylenol, which also contains acetaminophen. This duplication of active ingredients can lead to overmedication. Another scenario involves patients being prescribed or taking multiple drugs that produce the same or similar therapeutic effects. For instance, a patient using a prescription-strength ibuprofen product might also take a naproxen product, whether prescription or OTC. This overlap can result in overmedication, posing risks to the patient’s health and increasing overall healthcare costs. Patients may also overmedicate themselves by taking their medications at shorter intervals than prescribed or indicated on the product label. This behavior can lead to the accumulation of medications in the body at higher-than-intended levels, potentially causing serious or even fatal side effects.
